questions.q: The Boolean expression $\sim(p \vee q) \vee(\sim p \wedge q)$ is equivalent to
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \text {  Given, } \sim(p \vee q) \vee(\sim p \wedge q) \\ & \Rightarrow(\sim p \wedge \sim q) \vee(\sim p \wedge q) \text { (By De Morgan's Law) } \\ & \Rightarrow \sim p \wedge(\sim q \vee q) \text { (Distributive Law) } \\ & \Rightarrow \sim p \wedge t \text { (By complement law, where } t=\text { tautology) } \\ & \Rightarrow \sim p \text { (Identity law) }\end{aligned}$

questions.q:
Let $p, q, r$ be three logical statements. Consider the compound statements
$S_1:((\sim p) \vee q) \vee((\sim p) \vee r)$ and
$S_2: p \rightarrow(q \vee r)$
Then, which of the following is NOT true?
options: If $S_2$ is true, then $S_1$ is true
If $S_2$ is false, then $S_1$ is false
If $S_2$ is false, then $S_1$ is true
If $S_1$ is false, then $S_2$ is false
questions.solution:
Given statement $S_1:(\sim p \vee q) \vee(\sim p \vee r)\equiv \sim p \vee(q \vee r)S_2: p \rightarrow(q \vee r)\equiv \sim p \vee(q \vee r) \rightarrow$ By conditional law
$S_1 \equiv S_2$

questions.q: The negation of the Boolean expression $((\sim q)\wedge p) \Rightarrow((\sim p) \vee q)$ is logically equivalent to
questions.solution:
Given boolen expression are
$\begin{aligned} \\ & \sim p \vee q \equiv p \rightarrow q \text { and } \sim q \wedge p \equiv \sim(p \rightarrow q) \\ \\ & \text { Negation of } \sim(p \rightarrow q) \rightarrow(p \rightarrow q) \\ \\ & \text { is } \sim(p \rightarrow q) \wedge(\sim(p \rightarrow q)) \text { i.e., } \sim(p \rightarrow q) \\ \end{aligned}$

questions.q: Negation of the Boolean expression $\mathrm{p} \Leftrightarrow(\mathrm{q} \Rightarrow \mathrm{p})$ is
questions.solution:
Given expression is $p \Leftrightarrow(q \Rightarrow p)$
$\sim(\mathrm{p} \leftrightarrow(\mathrm{q} \rightarrow \mathrm{p}))$
$\sim(\mathrm{p} \leftrightarrow \mathrm{q})=(\mathrm{p} \wedge \sim \mathrm{q}) \vee(\mathrm{q} \wedge \sim \mathrm{p})$
$\sim(\mathrm{p} \leftrightarrow(\mathrm{q} \rightarrow \mathrm{p}))=(\mathrm{p} \wedge \sim(\mathrm{q} \rightarrow \mathrm{p})) \vee((\mathrm{q} \rightarrow \mathrm{p}) \wedge \sim \mathrm{p})$
$(\mathrm{p} \wedge \sim(\mathrm{q} \rightarrow \mathrm{p}))=\mathrm{p} \wedge(\mathrm{q} \wedge \sim \mathrm{p})=(p \wedge \sim p) \wedge q=c$
$(q \rightarrow p) \wedge \sim p=(\sim q \vee p) \wedge \sim p=\sim p \wedge(\sim q \vee p)$
$=(\sim \mathrm{p} \wedge \sim \mathrm{q}) \vee(\sim \mathrm{p} \wedge \mathrm{p})=\sim \mathrm{p} \wedge \sim \mathrm{q}$
$\sim(p \leftrightarrow(\dot{q} \rightarrow p))=c \vee(\sim p \wedge \sim q)=\sim p \wedge \sim q$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Negation of "Paris in France and London is in England" is
options: Paris is in England and London is in France
Paris is not in France or London is not in England
Paris is in England or London is in France
questions.solution:
Let \(p\) : Paris is in France, \(q\) : London is in England
\(\therefore \quad\) we have \(p \wedge q\)
Its negation is \(\sim(p \wedge q)=\sim p \vee \sim q\)
i.e., Paris is not in France or London is not in England.
